newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish opposition poised to win election, polls say.
newsitem.headline: Irish opposition poised to win election, polls say.

text.p: Irish voters are poised to change their government in Friday's election, according to the latest opinion poll which showed the centre-right opposition alliance well ahead of the ruling "rainbow coalition".

A day before the country's two million voters go to the polls, the survey in Thursday's Irish Independent newspaper put support for the alliance of Fianna Fail and the smaller Progressive Democrats at 49 percent, nine points ahead of the centre-left three-party coalition of Prime Minister John Bruton.

Bruton's rainbow coalition was pinning its hopes on winning over the 14 percent of voters yet to make up their minds, after a television debate between Bruton and Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern late on Wednesday which Bruton was widely considered to have won.

"John Bruton put in the best performance of his political life in the grand debate of would-be taoisigh (prime ministers) on television last night," the Irish Times said. "He left Mr Bertie Ahern, the most popular leader in this election campaign, for dead."

Bruton was even considered to have held his own on the thorny subject of Northern Ireland, an issue usually thought to favour Fianna Fail which has always claimed to be the authentic voice of Irish republicans who want to unite British-ruled Northern Ireland with the Irish Republic.
Ahern accused Bruton of allowing the Anglo-Irish peace initiative on Northern Ireland to grind to a halt during his 2-1/2 year tenure.

"The peace process has stalled under this government," he said, pledging to "stand up" for the rights of Northern Ireland's Catholic minority against the British government and the pro-British Protestant Unionists.
But Bruton, who has faced criticism for appearing too sympathetic to the Unionists, said Northern Ireland's Protestants were Irish people too and needed befriending.
"I believe the Unionists are Irish people and the Irish taoiseach has to befriend them as Irish people," he said. "It is not a question of religion."
His remarks risked the wrath of both nationalist voters and the Unionists, who consider themselves to be British, but newspapers said he had scored well on the issue in the debate.
Both Bruton and Ahern agreed that the Irish Republican Army (IRA) had to call a ceasefire in its 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland before a breakthrough could be made.
The IRA's Sinn Fein political representatives are barred from peace talks because the guerrillas have failed to renew a 17-month truce they ended in February 1996.

The Fianna Fail/Progressive Democrat alliance has been consistently ahead in opinion polls throughout the three-week election campaign, but Thursday's survey showed it gaining support as the election neared.

Financial markets have taken the campaign in their stride since both alliances are committed to continue Ireland's economic boom and to be among the first members of economic and monetary union (EMU).
But if neither coalition wins a clear victory, the markets could be unsettled by a hung parliament until the shape of the next government emerges after inter-party bargaining.
The poll was conducted on Tuesday with 1,110 people interviewed. Previous opinion polls suggested a hung parliament.
But the 49-percent support indicated in the latest opinion poll would be enough to win the opposition alliance a workable parliamentary majority, the Irish Independent said.
The poll also showed 53 percent were satisfied with the present government, but voters still seemed to want a change. Ireland has not re-elected a government in almost 30 years.
"The poll underlines a startling reality -- a successful government well regarded by more than half of voters stares defeat in the face," the Independent said.
